evaluation.positioning_hook: After his family is massacred by a criminal clan, a grief-stricken Catholic father hunts the surviving brothers while his cop sister races to stop him from becoming the next body.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The revenge-crime engine is immediately legible and the emotional stakes are clear, but the script’s heavy Catholic theology, long grief passages, and brutal violence narrow the audience beyond a broad commercial crowd.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early: Jacob’s family is murdered by the Risaldis, and the story becomes a race between his vigilante justice and Jodie’s attempt to stop him. The opening massacre and the later alley/club confrontations make the engine easy to explain in one breath.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jacob and Jodie are both emotionally loaded, and Ethan gives the script a compelling moral counterweight. Victor and Martin are vivid antagonists, though several supporting family members function more as pressure points than fully independent characters.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s Catholic framework is not decorative; confession, adoration, penance, and sacramental imagery are built into the spine of the story. That gives the revenge thriller a distinct identity, even when the underlying crime plot is familiar.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps escalating through funerals, raids, alley fights, hotel deaths, and the final mansion showdown. It does occasionally pause for thematic dialogue and devotional reflection, which slows the propulsion between major set pieces.

resonant_originality.reasoning: A Catholic grief story that turns into a family-vs-family crime purge feels specific and memorable, especially with confession booth framing and hymn-driven transitions. The core revenge structure is familiar, but the spiritual register makes it feel newly inflected.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world has a strong social texture: police bureaucracy, church ritual, criminal hierarchy, mayoral spin, and the family’s internal purity cult all create pressure. The Risaldi mansion, the club, the docks, and the church each feel like distinct nodes in the same ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very clear tonal identity: operatic, devotional, and brutal at once. It moves between domestic tenderness, religious consolation, and graphic violence in a way that feels authored rather than generic.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real thematic layers around guilt, absolution, inherited violence, and the difference between justice and vengeance. The script keeps returning to those ideas through confession, therapy, and Father Michael, which suggests more beneath the surface than a standard revenge piece.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jacob/Jodie, Jacob/Ethan, Ethan/Martin, and Victor/the family all generate recurring tension, and the story keeps recombining those pairings. It is still anchored by a few dominant relationships rather than a truly elastic ensemble machine.

lead_characters.name: Jacob Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 30s to early 40s, Catholic, working-class father and brother, white.
lead_characters.hook: A devastated family man whose faith is the only thing left standing after his wife and children are slaughtered. Jacob is tender, volatile, and increasingly dangerous; he wants justice, but what he actually has is grief with a pulse. The script tracks him from broken survivor to man willing to cross the line, then asks whether confession can still reach him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Casey Affleck in Manchester by the Sea or Joel Edgerton in The Gift: a contained, grief-saturated lead who can carry silence, rage, and moral collapse in the same frame. It gives an actor the chance to play interior devastation and then detonate it.

lead_characters.name: Jodie Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 30s, police officer, Catholic, white.
lead_characters.hook: Jacob’s sister and the story’s moral counterweight, Jodie is a cop who is competent enough to chase monsters but emotionally wrecked enough to understand them. She is hard-edged at work, soft and frayed in private, and the script uses her as both investigator and family witness. Her conflict is that she wants to save Jacob while also needing him to survive her own grief.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Amy Ryan in Gone Baby Gone or Regina King in If Beale Street Could Talk real emotional authority: a woman with professional command and private collapse. It offers a strong actor the chance to play authority, guilt, and sibling love without ever becoming ornamental.

lead_characters.name: Ethan Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, criminal family member, morally conflicted, white.
lead_characters.hook: The Risaldi brother who can still hear his conscience, Ethan is the family’s weak link and the story’s most interesting internal defector. He is terrified, principled, and desperate to believe he can save someone inside a system built to erase mercy. He becomes the bridge between the police and the family, but never fully escapes either side.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Jesse Plemons in The Power of the Dog: a haunted, morally split man whose face does half the writing. It gives an actor a chance to play fear, intelligence, and spiritual exhaustion in a role that keeps shifting allegiance.

lead_characters.name: Victor Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Victor is the family’s authoritarian engine, a patriarch who treats cruelty as order and children as inventory. He is composed, theatrical, and terrifyingly certain that power justifies every atrocity. The script makes him less a gangster than a doctrine with a pulse.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad or Michael Gambon in The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover its voltage: a commanding, monstrous authority figure with language as a weapon. It’s a prestige villain part built for an actor who can make control feel like menace.

lead_characters.name: Martin Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Martin is the family’s most volatile son, a sadist who performs cruelty like theater and then collapses under his father’s judgment. He is loud, unstable, and deeply needy for approval, which makes him both dangerous and pitiable. The script gives him the most overtly monstrous behavior, but also enough shame to make him human.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Jack Gleeson did in Game of Thrones or Ben Mendelsohn did in Animal Kingdom: play a character who is both repellent and fascinating. It’s a high-wire villain part with room for panic, humiliation, and explosive violence.

lead_characters.name: Frankie Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, criminal family member, white.
lead_characters.hook: Frankie is the quieter brother, more frightened than feral, and that makes him dangerous in a different way. He wants to survive the family more than he wants to lead it, and the script uses him to show what obedience looks like when it starts to rot from the inside.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Tom Pelphrey in Ozark or Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire a lot of mileage: a subordinate who can crack under pressure and still feel alive. It offers a strong character actor a chance to play fear, loyalty, and collapse.

lead_characters.name: Edward Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, physically imposing criminal, white.
lead_characters.hook: Edward is the family’s blunt instrument, a mountain of muscle who does the dirty work without much visible interiority. He is less verbally expressive than Martin or Ethan, but the script uses him as the embodiment of the family’s physical threat. He is the kind of presence that makes every room feel smaller.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of a Michael Mando-type physical enforcer role: minimal speech, maximum menace, and a lot of behavioral storytelling. It gives an actor a chance to build character through posture, stillness, and sudden violence.

lead_characters.name: Alicia
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid 50s, Victor’s wife, former stripper, white.
lead_characters.hook: Alicia is trapped inside Victor’s orbit and knows exactly how little power she has in it. She is frightened, compliant on the surface, and quietly devastated underneath, which makes her one of the script’s clearest victims of the family system. Her scenes carry the cost of living inside Victor’s version of order.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects or Laura Linney in Ozark a lot of emotional weight: a woman whose restraint is the performance. It offers a seasoned actor a chance to play fear, humiliation, and buried resistance.

lead_characters.name: Father Michael
lead_characters.hook: Father Michael is the script’s spiritual ballast, a priest who speaks in parable, humor, and practical mercy. He is not naïve; he understands the violence around him, but he insists on grace as a discipline rather than a slogan. He gives the story its clearest language for redemption.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Brendan Gleeson in Calvary or Mark Ruffalo in Spotlight its quiet authority: a moral witness with warmth and steel. It’s a rich supporting part for an actor who can make wisdom feel lived-in rather than preachy.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: premium streaming / theatrical specialty crime drama
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: prestige specialty theatrical or premium-streaming launch with awards-adjacent positioning.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly interior, but the mansion, club, docks, church, police station, and multiple night exteriors create a real location count; the fire/smoke climax and repeated crowd scenes keep it above a simple contained indie.

casting.note: Jacob, Jodie, Ethan, and Victor all need strong, specific performers, and the Risaldi brothers require sharply differentiated physical and behavioral casting. The child roles also matter materially, especially Marcus and Jay in the family material.

development.note: The script’s Catholic framework, grief language, and revenge logic are distinctive, but the final act depends on balancing spiritual absolution against vigilante catharsis without losing either side of the premise.

comp_set.why_it_comps: A grief-driven lead performance anchors the movie, with trauma shaping every relationship and every choice.

comp_set.title: Prisoners
comp_set.why_it_comps: The story shares the same moral pressure-cooker energy: a family crisis, a criminal underworld, and escalating acts of desperation.

comp_set.title: Calvary
comp_set.why_it_comps: The Catholic worldview is not window dressing; faith, confession, and moral injury are built into the dramatic engine.

comp_set.title: A History of Violence
comp_set.why_it_comps: A family man is forced back into violence, and the movie keeps asking what identity survives after blood is spilled.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like prestige crime dramas with emotional devastation, moral conflict, and a strong faith-inflected angle.
audience_target.demographics: 35-64 skew, slightly male-leaning but with strong female appeal through the sibling and family material; premium-cable and prestige-streaming audience.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, modest stunt work, and limited VFX keep it in indie feature territory, though the ensemble, night work, and climax add scope.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where character pain, moral consequence, and genre violence can coexist. The Catholic material gives it a differentiator that can help it stand out in a crowded crime field.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the script’s power is in the closed moral arc of Jacob, Jodie, and the Risaldi family, not in a sequel or spin-off engine.

strengths.what_it_means: The faith framework gives the movie a built-in identity that can separate it from standard revenge crime fare and make it easier to position as prestige rather than generic genre. That is attractive to buyers looking for elevated material and to actors who want roles with moral texture.
strengths.evidence: Confession booth scenes, adoration chapel scenes, Father Michael’s sermons, and the Act of Contrition structure all recur as story architecture.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jacob is a strong grief lead
strengths.what_it_means: The role offers a clear emotional engine and a real transformation path, which is exactly what can attract a serious actor and anchor audience empathy. It also gives the film a clean marketing promise: a father pushed past the edge by unbearable loss.
strengths.evidence: His therapy breakdown, the alley confrontation with Tyler, and the final breakdown in the ballroom all show a man moving from pain to action.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jodie gives the movie a second spine
strengths.what_it_means: The sister/cop dynamic broadens the emotional and commercial reach beyond a single revenge POV and creates a second lead-level performance opportunity. That helps the project in casting conversations and gives the film a more durable relationship engine.
strengths.evidence: Jodie’s police work, her grief at the funeral, and her repeated attempts to stop Jacob from crossing the line all create a parallel arc.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Risaldi family is a vivid villain system
strengths.what_it_means: Victor, Martin, Ethan, Frankie, and Edward are not interchangeable heavies; they each embody a different form of corruption, fear, or resistance. That makes the antagonistic world feel castable, memorable, and story-generating.
strengths.evidence: Victor’s ballroom discipline, Martin’s sadism, Ethan’s conscience, Frankie’s fear, and Edward’s physical brutality each play differently.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The climax is built for catharsis
strengths.what_it_means: The final mansion confrontation gives the movie a clear event ending that can satisfy genre buyers and audience expectations. It also creates a strong trailerable sequence with emotional and visual escalation.
strengths.evidence: The ballroom showdown, the gun standoff, the reveal of Katherine, and the final aftermath all stack into a big finish.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige crime feature with a real identity: Catholic grief, family trauma, and revenge all fused into one morally charged engine. It has the kind of lead role, sibling counterweight, and contained-enough production footprint that can attract serious actors and specialty buyers without needing tentpole scale.

items.area: The script leans hard on sermon scenes
items.detail: Father Michael’s confession, homily, and theology passages are distinctive, but they also slow the momentum between the crime beats. For some buyers, that will read as depth; for others, it will feel like the movie pauses to explain itself.

items.area: The violence is extreme and sustained
items.detail: The opening massacre, the child death, the alley killing, and the ballroom execution push the content into very dark territory. That narrows the audience to buyers comfortable with hard mature material and makes tone management a real conversation in packaging.

items.area: The music clearance list is real
items.detail: Come Back, O Holy Night, Clair de Lune, 500 Miles, Good Looking, and L’amour Toujours are all named on the page, and several are used as emotional punctuation. That means sync budgeting and clearance strategy are not optional line items.

items.area: The ensemble is vivid but not equally weighted
items.detail: Jacob, Jodie, Ethan, and Victor are strong anchors, but several Risaldi siblings function primarily as pressure or threat rather than fully dimensional engines. That is fine for a feature, but it means the movie’s value is concentrated in a few roles rather than spread across the cast.

items.area: The climax depends on a lot of moving parts
items.detail: The final mansion sequence requires Jacob, Jodie, Ethan, Victor, Marcus, and the police response to all land in sync, while the Katherine reveal adds a surreal emotional beat. It’s a strong finish, but it is also the section most dependent on precise staging and performance control.

issues.headline: The biggest friction is tonal and structural: the script wants to be both a propulsive revenge thriller and a faith-forward grief meditation, and it spends real page time on the latter. Add the explicit violence and the named-music clearance list, and this becomes a buyer for a specific lane rather than a broad one.
